newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Pakistan rejects linking labour with trade at WTO.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan rejects linking labour with trade at WTO.

text.p: Pakistan feels it abides by international labour standards and has rejected efforts to place this issue on the World Trade Organisation (WTO) agenda, Pakistan's trade minister said on Thursday.
"Pakistan fully adheres to the internationally recognised core labour standards....we have rules that enforce that," said Dr Mohammad Zubair Khan, Pakistan's minister for trade.
He said there were several institutions that watched over standards and enforced labour regulations in Pakistan.
Ministers and delegates attending the inaugural ministerial conference of the WTO in Singapore have been hotly debating whether labour issues should be linked with trade this week.
"The issue is not whether any particular country believes in these standards, but whether WTO is the relevant organisation to handle this," the minister said.
He added that if such issues were brought to the WTO, it would result in "burdening" the trade organisation, "hindering the multilateral free trading system."

Asked about including a labour statement in the WTO's final declaration, which some countries like the United States have been pushing for, he hinted Pakistan had softened its stance on this, adding "every country has to accommodate to reach consensus."
Trade delegates noted one of the "compromises" on labour was a proposal that the chairman of the Singapore meeting make a statement on labour, and not the director-general of the conference.
But one member of the Pakistan delegation admitted there were legal differences involved.

"We believe that the chairman's statement on any issue covers the issues that have been raised by members at the conference and does not necessarily mean follow-up action, or a commitment by the ministers of the contents of the issue."

Pakistan, facing scathing international criticism and threats of trade sanctions, has taken steps to curb child labour, but officials have said previously total elimination was impossible due to high poverty and illiteracy rates.

No official figures are available, but a survey carried out by the Labour Ministry in collaboration with the International Labour Organisation, released in October, said 3.6 million children aged five to 14 were working full-time in Pakistan.
